wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e111.summary: Poses the question whether in every demonstration a definition is the middle term. Argument for yes from Posterior Analytics II: every question is a question about the middle, and middle and cause are the same. So every question concerns a definition as middle, and since every demonstrable conclusion can be asked about, each is concluded through a definition.
claims: Every question concerns the middle term (argument).
Middle and cause are the same (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e129.summary: Argument to the contrary: as said before, some property is demonstrated of God, and something of being, yet not through a definition, since neither God nor being has one.
claims: Some properties are demonstrated of God and of being without a definition as middle.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e138.summary: Reports the common opinion that the middle in every demonstration is a definition, and introduces a particular opinion about demonstratio potissima: that its middle is the definition of the property, not of the subject. The opinion will explain what demonstratio potissima is and why its middle is the property's definition.
claims: Common opinion: the middle of every demonstration is a definition (reported).
On one opinion, the middle of demonstratio potissima is the definition of the property (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e156.summary: The opinion explains demonstratio potissima through Aristotle's five conditions (propter quid, first figure, universal, affirmative, ostensive) and a sixth from Book II: its middle is a formal definition, taken from form or end rather than from matter or efficient cause. It argues that the middle is not the subject's definition. Demonstrations through any kind of cause go through a cause of inherence, but the subject's formal definition is not the formal cause of the property's inherence; it is rather efficient or material.
claims: Demonstratio potissima is propter quid, first-figure, universal, affirmative and ostensive (reported).
Its middle is a formal definition taken from form or end (reported).
The subject's formal definition is not the formal cause of the property's inherence (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e190.summary: Second argument of the opinion: the middle of demonstratio potissima must be the proper and proximate cause of the property's inherence. The subject's formal definition is not, since it is the proper, exemplary and proximate cause of the subject itself.
claims: The middle of demonstratio potissima must be the proper and proximate cause of inherence (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e208.summary: Third argument of the opinion: the middle must be middle by nature, not only by position. The subject's formal definition is prior by nature to the subject and so does not stand naturally between subject and predicate. It then argues from Posterior Analytics II, as read by Grosseteste, that demonstration through the formal cause is the most powerful, since end causes efficient and form causes matter. It answers the 'causes are mutually causes' objection by ranking the causes: the end causes the efficient; the efficient causes only becoming; matter causes only as an occasion after being constituted by form. Form makes the thing to be whatever it is per se, so the definition from form is the best middle.
claims: The middle must be naturally intermediate between subject and predicate (reported).
The end causes the efficient cause and form causes matter (reported).
Form is the most powerful cause, so the definition from form is the best middle (reported).
The efficient cause causes only the becoming of a thing (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e286.summary: The opinion's argument that the property's definition is the middle: it is the formal exemplary, proper and proximate cause of the property, posterior by nature to the subject and prior to the property, as measure to measured. So it stands naturally between subject and predicate.
claims: The property's definition is its formal exemplary cause (reported).
The property's definition is naturally between subject and property (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e302.summary: Ockham argues against the opinion. If the property's definition were the middle, it would be either a definition properly speaking, through intrinsic principles, or one by addition. Not the first, since many properties lack such definitions, namely all that import simple absolute things.
claims: Properties importing simple absolute things have no definition through intrinsic principles.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e318.summary: Nor a definition by addition: such a definition includes either the subject itself or some extrinsic cause. If the subject, it cannot be a middle, because a middle must not contain either extreme. If an extrinsic cause, the demonstration is not universal, as shown in the previous question.
claims: A middle term may not contain either extreme.
Demonstration through an extrinsic cause is not universal.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e342.summary: Further: demonstratio potissima proceeds from premises indemonstrable a priori, but the property's definition is demonstrable a priori of the subject, since on the opponents' view the subject causes the property and its form and so causes knowledge of the definition expressing that form. So it cannot be a principle in demonstratio potissima.
claims: Demonstratio potissima proceeds from premises indemonstrable a priori.
On the opponents' own view the property's definition is demonstrable a priori of the subject.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e365.summary: Further: a definition does not really differ from what it defines and so is not really its cause, but demonstratio potissima is through a cause.
claims: A definition does not differ really from the defined.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e374.summary: The opinion's reply: definition and defined differ not only verbally but by a 'thing of reason'. The name signifies a confused whole (circle), while the definition divides it into its parts, and this explication belongs to the definition's significate. So the definition is the measure and exemplar of the defined.
claims: The definition explicates what the name signifies confusedly (reported).
Definition and defined differ by a thing of reason (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e396.summary: Ockham counters: whether or not definition and defined differ, the definition always explicates the real cause of what the defined imports. A simple absolute property has only extrinsic real causes, so the definition serving as middle would be taken from an extrinsic cause and not be the formal definition the opponents mean. He also argues that they misread Aristotle's formal/material distinction: every definition of something with matter and form must express both, otherwise it would not convert with the defined, since what expresses only form is predicated of the form in the abstract.
claims: Simple absolute properties have only extrinsic real causes.
Every definition of a hylomorphic thing must express both matter and form.
A definition expressing only form would not convert with the composite.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e433.summary: Attacks the opinion's metaphysics of causes. 'The end causes the efficient' and 'form causes matter' are either metaphorical or false: otherwise something would cause God, an efficient cause; the sun would be caused by its ends; and the soul acting for a bad end would be caused by that end. 'Form causes formally when the efficient ceases' holds of secondary efficient causes, not of the first, so the first efficient cause would be the best middle. 'Matter causes the composite only after being constituted by form' is contradictory, since matter is informed only in causing the whole. And matter belongs to the essence of the composite; otherwise a substantial form would be per se in a species and genus.
claims: 'The end causes the efficient cause' is metaphorical or false.
Form does not continue to cause without the first efficient cause.
Matter belongs to the essence of the composite.
A substantial form alone is not per se in a species or genus.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e488.summary: Ockham's first thesis: demonstratio potissima is propter quid, universal (in both senses explained earlier) and affirmative. Being universal affirmative, it follows that it is in the first figure. Being propter quid, it is through a cause. Being precisely affirmative, it is ostensive.
claims: Demonstratio potissima is propter quid, universal and affirmative.
The other conditions (first figure, through a cause, ostensive) follow from these three.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e504.summary: Second thesis: sometimes the middle of a demonstration is a definition and sometimes not. A definition is middle when the angle-sum property is shown of the triangle or corruptibility of composite substance. It is not when 'susceptible of learning' is shown of man through the intellective soul rather than through man's definition, granting that it belongs to the soul alone.
claims: The middle of demonstration is sometimes a definition and sometimes not.
'Man is susceptible of learning' is demonstrated through the intellective soul, not man's definition.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e521.summary: Proves the second thesis. Demonstratio potissima proceeds from simply indemonstrable premises, but the proposition predicating the property of man's definition is not simply first, since the one predicating it of the soul (its first subject) is prior. Also, the middle must contain only what is causally relevant, while man's definition includes parts (body) that do nothing for the property's inherence, which would be a non-causa ut causa fallacy.
claims: Predicating susceptibility to learning of man's definition is not a first proposition.
The middle of demonstratio potissima should contain only what is causally relevant.
Using man's definition here commits the fallacy of non-cause as cause.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e550.summary: Third thesis: when the middle is a definition, it is the subject's definition, not the property's. Such a definition must express the cause, something necessarily required for predicating the property, and the subject's definition expresses parts without which the property could not belong (the triangle's lines; the separable parts of composite substance for corruptibility). Such demonstrations are mathematical. Because mathematics holds first place among demonstrations, Aristotle often attributes to demonstration in general conditions that hold always or mostly of mathematical ones.
claims: When a definition is the middle, it is the subject's definition, not the property's.
The subject's definition expresses parts necessary for the property.
Aristotle attributes to demonstration generally conditions proper to mathematical demonstration.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e587.summary: Answers the opinion's first argument: it rests on the false imagination that a property or its inherence has a formal cause. A simple form can have only efficient or final causes, not material (matter causes the whole, not the form) or formal (it is itself a form and has no form to define it by). If 'cause of inherence' is meant, the inherence relation depends equally on foundation and term, so both definitions would serve as middle. If 'cause of the property' is meant, the only cause is the subject, so the subject's definition is the middle.
claims: A simple form has only efficient or final causes.
Matter causes the composite, not the form.
A relation of inherence depends essentially on both foundation and term.
The subject is the cause of the property, so its definition is the middle.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e642.summary: Answers the second argument: the middle must express a proximate cause, chiefly in the genus of material cause, since it must be the property's subject. That is either the first subject (when demonstrating of a non-first subject) or a definition expressing the subject's essential parts, not the property's definition, which expresses the property rather than its cause. The middle need not be a proper cause excluding other effects. The intellective soul can be middle for showing that man is intellective and volitional, being the immediate subject of both acts and also man's formal cause.
claims: The middle must express a proximate cause, chiefly material, namely the subject.
The property's definition expresses the property, not its cause.
One cause can be the middle for several properties.
The intellective soul is the immediate subject of intellection and volition and the formal cause of man.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e686.summary: Answers the third argument: there must be some real order between the middle and the extremes, not merely of position. Sometimes the middle is simply first in that order: the intellective soul is prior by nature to man, since a part can exist without the whole and not the reverse, and the whole subject is in a way prior to an accident. In the order of perfection, however, the soul may be strictly intermediate: man is more perfect than the soul, and the soul more perfect than its acts.
claims: A real order, not merely positional, must hold between middle and extremes.
A part is prior by nature to its whole because it can exist without it.
In order of perfection the soul lies between man and its acts.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e721.summary: Raises an objection: a single subject cannot have several equally first properties; one is always prior and is the reason for demonstrating the others.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e731.summary: Replies that a subject can have several equally first properties, neither of which is the reason for demonstrating the other, though one may ground the other in a particular, qualified demonstration. One grounds another in universal demonstration only when it imports the other's subject, or signifies something existing in the subject to which the second property first belongs. Examples: if quantity is a thing distinct from substance and the subject of qualities, quantity mediates quality-properties of substance; heat mediates 'calefactive' of fire.
claims: A subject can have several equally first properties.
One property grounds another in universal demonstration only if it imports the other's subject.
Heat is the middle for demonstrating 'calefactive' of fire.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e770.summary: Answers the opinion's claim that the formal definition is the middle: when a definition is middle in universal demonstration it is the subject's formal definition. It is called formal not because it includes only the form but because it includes the thing's essential principles.
claims: In universal demonstration the subject's formal definition is the middle.
A definition is 'formal' because it includes essential principles, not only the form.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e786.summary: To interpret Aristotle, notes the basic division of definitions into those indicating quid rei and those indicating quid nominis.
claims: Definitions are either quid rei or quid nominis.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e793.summary: Develops the distinction. A formal definition is through essential principles; strictly it fits only composite substance, broadly also things with distinct parts of the same kind, as in mathematics (triangle as a figure contained by three lines). A material definition is through extrinsic principles, matter being extended to any receptacle, and such definitions usually express only quid nominis. Eclipse as privation of the moon's light by the earth's interposition, and thunder as sound from fire extinguished in a cloud, are nominal: the same effect from another cause would not be so named. In general, definitions through extrinsic causes are nominal, since a definition converts formally with the defined, but God could produce any thing without its extrinsic cause, which would break the inference.
claims: Formal definitions are through essential principles; strictly only composite substances have them.
Mathematical objects have formal definitions in a broad sense.
Definitions through extrinsic causes express only quid nominis.
Definitions of eclipse and thunder are nominal.
Since God can produce any thing without its extrinsic cause, a definition through an extrinsic cause cannot convert formally with a real thing.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e895.summary: Concludes that a formal definition is always given through intrinsic and essential principles, or rather concepts expressing them, while a material definition is given through what is extrinsic to the thing to which the definition first belongs.
claims: Formal definitions are through concepts of intrinsic principles.
Material definitions are through extrinsic principles.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e906.summary: Shows this is Aristotle's intent. In 'the cause is either the same or other', 'same' cannot mean really identical, since cause and effect are never really the same. It means intrinsic cause, which is 'not simply other', as the Commentator says a part is not simply other than the whole. Matter is as intrinsic as form, though form is the principal part. Aristotle calls definitions 'according to species' those not given through another cause, and those through other causes 'material'. Definitions according to species have no middle by which they are demonstrated, while material ones can.
claims: Cause and effect are never really the same.
An intrinsic cause is 'the same' in the sense of not simply other than the whole.
Matter is as intrinsic to the composite as form.
Definitions according to species are not demonstrated through a middle.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e955.summary: Draws consequences about definitions and demonstration. A definition expressing quid rei can never be demonstrated of the defined, since that proposition is immediate. If a simple thing had a real definition, it would be demonstrable not of the defined but of whatever the defined is demonstrable of, through the same middle. So if heat had a definition through intrinsic principles, it would be demonstrable of what heat is demonstrable of and would be a demonstrative conclusion in that sense.
claims: A real definition is never demonstrable of its definiendum.
A real definition is demonstrable of whatever the definiendum is demonstrable of.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e992.summary: Distinguishes two senses of a nominal definition: (1) the expression everyone using the name understands by it; (2) an expression whose truth follows from the truth of the first.
claims: Nominal definitions are either the commonly understood expression or one derived from it.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1003.summary: The first kind of nominal definition cannot be demonstrated of the defined, though it can be of the subject, and is a principle of demonstration. The second can be demonstrated. Example: everyone understands by 'house' something protecting us from cold and storms. From that, together with the assumption that only wood and stones could protect us, it follows that a house is composed of solid bodies, of wood and stones. So a second definition that expresses no quid rei can be demonstrated through the first and be a conclusion.
claims: The primary nominal definition is a principle, not demonstrable of the defined.
A secondary nominal definition can be demonstrated from the primary one.
Material composition of a house can be derived from its functional definition.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1040.summary: From these one can compose a complex definition expressing all the thing's necessary causes, end and matter, but not the efficient cause, since it does not matter for the principal nominal definition which agent produced it, as it matters what matter it is made of. Likewise, everyone understands by 'demonstration' a syllogism producing knowledge, which requires necessary propositions; hence the definition 'demonstration is a syllogism from true... premises'.
claims: A complex definition can express end and matter but not the efficient cause.
The efficient cause is irrelevant to verifying the principal nominal definition.
The definition of demonstration is derived from its nominal definition.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1060.summary: Cautions that such derivations are not universal demonstrations simpliciter. Aristotle accordingly calls them 'a logical syllogism of the what-it-is', not demonstration. Similarly, a real definition can be in a way inferred from a nominal one: assuming 'man' means a composite substance able to understand and will, one can conclude that it is composed of body and intellective soul. These inferences do not produce scientia but only infer conclusions from premises, since according to Posterior Analytics II one cannot know what something is without knowing that it is.
claims: Derivations from nominal definitions are logical syllogisms, not universal demonstrations.
A quid rei can be inferred from a quid nominis.
One cannot know what something is without knowing that it is.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1093.summary: Objection: then whoever did not know that an eclipse exists would not know what an eclipse is.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1099.summary: Ockham accepts the principle as Aristotle means it: one cannot naturally know what something is without knowing that it is, was or will be, since otherwise one could not naturally know it to be possible or that its nominal definition is non-contradictory. Knowing the quid is the same as knowing the cause of its existence. Apart from intuitive cognition, and what it immediately causes, one cannot naturally know that a property exists or will exist without knowing that its cause does. With intuitive cognition one can know the moon is eclipsed without knowing the cause or the causal definition. Abstractively, one knows it only through the cause (the earth's interposition).
claims: One cannot naturally know what something is without knowing it exists, existed or will exist.
Knowledge of possibility depends on knowledge of existence at some time.
Apart from intuitive cognition, a property's existence is known only through its cause.
Intuitive cognition gives knowledge of an eclipse without knowledge of its cause.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1136.summary: Raises an objection: abstractive cognition abstracts from existence.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1141.summary: Further objections: abstractive cognition cannot cause knowledge of contingent truth, and 'the moon is or will be eclipsed' is contingent.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1148.summary: Answers the first objection: abstractive cognition abstracts from existence in that it alone does not suffice to know existence at a determinate time. With other knowledge it can suffice: in Aristotle's way one can know that the moon will be eclipsed at a set time by knowing how sun and moon will move and so that the earth will interpose. Such knowledge is always through the cause.
claims: Abstractive cognition alone does not suffice to know existence at a determinate time.
With other knowledge, abstractive cognition can yield knowledge of future existence through causes.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1166.summary: Answers the second objection: in the same way, through such truths a contingent truth can be known, so abstractive cognition of the terms alone does not suffice.
claims: Contingent truths can be known abstractively by means of other truths.
Abstractive cognition of the terms alone does not suffice for contingent truth.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1182.summary: Answers the third objection: a necessary proposition can be formed from those terms and known by scientia proprie dicta, while the contingent proposition can be evidently known though not known by scientia proprie dicta.
claims: A necessary proposition about eclipses can be formed and known scientifically.
A contingent proposition can be evidently known without being known by scientia proprie dicta.

wo8uy7-d1e118-d1e1192.summary: Answers the principal argument: cause and middle are the same if 'cause' is extended to whatever the property first belongs to and without which it could not belong to another, in universal propter quid demonstration. 'The why and the what-it-is are the same' does not mean the cause is the whole definition, but that the cause is placed in the definition. Aristotle's eclipse example shows the earth's interposition is only part of the definition 'privation of light from the moon by the earth's interposition'. The paragraph ends by announcing a further annexed question.
claims: Cause and middle are the same if 'cause' covers whatever the property first belongs to.
'The why and the what are the same' means that the cause is part of the definition.

wo8uy7-d1e118.summary: Prologue question 5, annexed to the second principal question, asks whether a definition is the middle term in every demonstration. Ockham rejects the opinion that the middle of demonstratio potissima is the property's formal definition. Simple properties lack intrinsic definitions; definitions by addition contain an extreme or an extrinsic cause; the opponents' own principles make the property's definition demonstrable; and their hierarchy of causes (end causing the efficient, form causing matter) is metaphorical or false. His own view: demonstratio potissima is propter quid, universal and affirmative, from which its other conditions follow. Its middle is sometimes a definition and sometimes not (the intellective soul for susceptibility to learning), and when it is a definition, it is the subject's definition expressing the essential parts on which the property depends, as in mathematics. He then develops a theory of definition: formal definitions through intrinsic principles versus material ones through extrinsic causes, which are only nominal, since God could produce a thing without its extrinsic cause. Real definitions are never demonstrable of their definienda, and secondary nominal definitions can be derived from primary ones by 'logical syllogism'. Knowing what something is requires knowing that it is, and he clarifies the roles of intuitive and abstractive cognition in knowing contingent events such as eclipses.
claims: Not every demonstration has a definition as its middle.
When the middle is a definition, it is the subject's, not the property's.
Definitions through extrinsic causes express only quid nominis.
A real definition is never demonstrable of what it defines.
Knowledge of quid est presupposes knowledge of si est.
Intuitive cognition can give knowledge of an event without knowledge of its cause.
